title: Lister's antiseptic surgery

confidence.note: Lister's own 1867 papers fix the dates, from the first carbolic dressing in August 1865 to publication in 1867. That antisepsis cut wound infection is accepted; how quickly and why it spread is debated, and historians now stress that his critics had serious reasons for doubt.

people: Joseph Lister (1827–1912), professor of surgery at Glasgow
James Greenlees, boy whose compound fracture was the first case Lister reported
Thomas Anderson (1819–1874), Glasgow chemist who pointed Lister to Pasteur's work
summary: A Glasgow surgeon read Pasteur, reasoned that germs rot wounds, and dressed a boy's shattered leg in carbolic acid. Making the idea stick took decades.
body: On 12 August 1865 an eleven-year-old boy, James Greenlees, was admitted to the Glasgow Royal Infirmary with a compound fracture of the leg: the broken bone had pierced the skin. Such wounds commonly festered, and the usual outcome was amputation or death. Joseph Lister dressed the wound with a pad soaked in carbolic acid. It did not suppurate.

Lister was acting on a borrowed idea. The Glasgow chemist Thomas Anderson had introduced him to Louis Pasteur's work showing that fermentation and putrefaction were caused by living organisms carried in the air, not by oxygen itself. If so, Lister reasoned, wounds need not be sealed from the air; it was enough to kill the "floating particles" with a chemical dressing.

He published in *The Lancet* in the spring of 1867, in four weekly articles describing eleven compound fractures, failures included, followed by a fifth on abscesses. Later that year he told the British Medical Association in Dublin that his two wards, once among the unhealthiest in the infirmary, had gone nine months without a single case of pyemia, hospital gangrene or erysipelas.

Acceptance was slow. A leading Leeds surgeon, Thomas Nunneley, reported that his colleagues had tried the method and given it up. Lister kept changing his materials, carbolic acid itself irritated tissue, and the germ theory behind it was not yet proven. Historians now argue that every part of the system was contested for good reasons, not out of ignorance.

The next step came from Germany. Robert Koch's laboratory found carbolic acid a weak germicide and Lister's spray useless, and surgeons turned to steam sterilization and keeping germs out of the wound altogether. In 1890 Ernst von Bergmann announced that his clinic had replaced antisepsis with asepsis, the principle of the modern operating room.

myth.tradition: Lister's critics were hidebound reactionaries who refused to believe in germs, and his method was obviously right from the start.
myth.record: His contemporaries had real grounds for doubt: results varied, the technique kept changing and the bacteriology was unsettled. Much of his system, including the carbolic spray, was later dropped in favor of asepsis.

links.note: Lister applied Pasteur's account of putrefaction to wounds.
An earlier, unheeded attack on infection by cleanliness.
Koch's lab tests of disinfectants helped turn antisepsis into asepsis.

title: The thermometer and the fever chart

confidence.note: Wunderlich's treatise appeared in Leipzig in 1868 and in English in 1871. The figure of about 25,000 cases comes from later summaries of his work, and whether his 37 °C was too high, or body temperature has since fallen, is still argued.

people: Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich (1815–1877), Leipzig physician
Thomas Clifford Allbutt (1836–1925), Leeds physician who devised a short clinical thermometer
summary: A Leipzig doctor charted the temperatures of some 25,000 patients and turned fever from a feeling into a number, with 37 °C as the healthy norm.
body: In 1868 Carl Wunderlich of Leipzig published a treatise on temperature in disease, drawn from about 15 years of readings, some patients measured four to six times a day. Plotted on charts, he argued, fevers followed characteristic courses, while healthy temperature held steady near 37 °C. His thermometers were large and slow, sometimes needing 20 minutes; in Leeds, Clifford Allbutt's 15-centimeter clinical thermometer, made from 1867, gave a reading in about five. Modern studies put average healthy temperature somewhat lower.

myth.tradition: Normal body temperature is exactly 37 °C, or 98.6 °F.
myth.record: Wunderlich gave a normal range of about 36.2–37.5 °C, and a recent British study of more than 35,000 patients found a mean oral temperature of 36.6 °C.
